turns.question: Our surface site came back at pH 8.7 this morning. Is that out of range for our pod, or are we okay?
turns.answer:
I can't tell you whether 8.7 is out of range for your pod — this pod's configured thresholds aren't available to me here, so I can't judge the reading against them.

As general background (not your pod's limit): USGS guidance notes that "River waters not affected by contamination generally have a pH in the range of 6.5 to 8.5" 【15†"River waters not affected by contamination generally have a pH in the range of 6.5 to 8.5"】. That's a general description of typical waters, not a health standard or your pod's alert limit.

If you'd like, I can explain what pH measures or what factors the documents say affect pH readings.

A pH (potential of Hydrogen) probe measures the hydrogen ion activity in a liquid.

ions from the liquid being measured to defuse into the outer layer of the glass, while
larger ions remain in the solution. The difference in the concentration of hydrogen ions
(outside the probe vs. inside the probe) creates a VERY small current. This current
is proportional to the concentration of hydrogen ions in the liquid being measured.

2.2 	pH Electrodes
The pH electrode is a special type of ion-selective
electrode (ISE) that is designed specifically for the measure-
ment of H+ activity in aqueous solution (fig. 6.4–2). Because
pH measurements of natural waters are most commonly made
with glass bulb electrodes, other types of pH electrodes are
not discussed. Combination glass bulb electrodes are made in
a variety of shapes and sizes by many manufacturers, but all
operate on the same principles. Depending on use, the typical
useful life expectancy of pH electrodes used in environmental
field operation is approximately 12 to 18 months.
2.2.1 	How a Combination pH Electrode Works
Combination glass bulb electrodes contain both a pH
electrode and a reference electrode. The pH electrode gener-
ates an electrical potential that is proportional to the concen-
tration of hydrogen ions in the sample solution, whereas the
reference electrode generates a constant electrical potential.
The electrodes together form a complete electrical circuit;
when the diffusion of hydrogen ions across the glass bulb
membrane reaches equilibrium, no electrical current is present,
and the difference in electrical potential that exists between the
reference and the pH electrodes is related to the hydrogen ion
activity in the solution.
A glass bulb pH electrode has a thin porous glass mem-
brane (bulb) that separates the solution being measured from
the internal solution. When a pH electrode is immersed in a
solution, hydrogen ions are exchanged with the sodium ions
within the thin hydrated layer of the glass membrane until
equilibrium between the internal and external solutions is

## 5. Natural Cycles and Look-Alike Events

Rule these out before declaring a pollution event.

### 5.1 Diel (24-Hour) Cycle

- Pattern: DO and pH rise through daylight, peak in mid to late afternoon, and fall overnight to a
  minimum just before dawn. Temperature follows solar heating. ORP shows a weaker version of the
  same pattern, partly because of temperature.
- Diagnostic: DO and pH move in phase, repeat each day, and change smoothly.
- Danger window: The pre-dawn DO minimum. Low-oxygen events and fish kills most often occur
  between about 03:00 and 07:00 local time.
- Caution: Solar-powered DataPods are also most likely to experience low battery voltage in the
  pre-dawn hours. Check battery voltage before interpreting a pre-dawn anomaly (Section 7).

### 5.2 Tidal Cycle

- Pattern: Southern California has mixed semidiurnal tides, with two unequal high tides and two
  unequal low tides per day (the main lunar period is about 12.42 hours). Salinity, temperature, and
  turbidity oscillate with tidal exchange. Turbidity often peaks near maximum current.
- Diagnostic: The change repeats on the tidal clock, not the solar clock, and shifts by about 50
  minutes per day.
- Method: Compare readings to the same tidal phase in the baseline, or remove tidal signal with
  harmonic analysis.
- Sensor exposure: Shallow DataPods may be exposed or nearly exposed at extreme low tides,
  creating fault signatures (Section 7).

### 5.3 Coastal Upwelling (Major False Positive)

- Cause: Winds push surface water offshore, bringing cold, low-oxygen, high-CO₂ deep water to the
  surface. In Southern California, upwelling is strongest in spring (roughly March through June) but
  can occur at other times.
- Signature: Temperature strongly down (2 to 6 °C over one to three days), DO down, pH down,
  salinity slightly up (about 0.1 to 0.3 PSU), ORP slightly down, turbidity little change.
- Why it matters: DO and pH fall together, which resembles organic pollution.
- Diagnostic: Temperature falls with DO and pH. Pollution does not cool the water. Salinity rises
  slightly instead of falling. The pattern often affects several nearby sites at once.

pH of surface waters is affected diurnally by photosynthe-
sis and respiration of algae and rooted macrophytes (Hem,
1989). Additionally, pH directly affects physiological func-
tions of biota and is an important indicator of the health of an
aquatic system.
The pH of water is defined as the negative base-10 loga-
rithm of the hydrogen ion activity {H+}.

Information on pH—
• In aqueous solutions, the hydrogen ion (H+) exists as
hydronium (H3O+). For simplicity, “H+” is commonly
used when defining pH.
• Potentiometric measurements made by using ion-
selective electrodes (ISE) indicate free ionic activities
rather than the actual concentrations of ions. Therefore,
similar to other ion-selective electrodes (ISE), pH elec-
trodes measure hydrogen ion activity.
• Activity can be thought of as an “effective” concentra-
tion and differs from true molar concentration because
of ion-ion interactions. The hydrogen ion activity is
defined as the molar concentration of hydrogen ions
multiplied by an activity coefficient that takes into
account the interaction of hydrogen ions with other
chemical species in the solution. For dilute waters,
activity values of ions are similar to their molar
concentrations. For waters with high ionic strength—
for example, brackish water or seawater—activities
can differ substantially from molar concentrations. The
theoretical basis of activity and activity coefficients
and their relation to ionic strength and ionic concen-
trations are described in detail in Hem (1989) and
Benjamin (2015).
• Activity is dimensionless; therefore, pH values are
unitless.
• Because pH is based on a logarithmic scale, a change
of 1 pH unit is a 10-fold change in the hydrogen ion
activity.
• Temperature and dissolved gases affect the chemi-
cal equilibria of ionic activities in aqueous solutions,
including that of H+ (Hem, 1989). For example, the
neutral pH of pure water at 25 degrees Celsius (°C) is
defined as 7.00, but the value is 6.92 at 30 °C and 7.48
at 0 °C. In addition, pure water in equilibrium with the
atmosphere at 25 °C has a pH of 5.7 because of the
dissolution and dissociation of carbon dioxide (CO2)
from the atmosphere.
• For an in-depth discussion of pH theory, see
Bates (1965).
• Figure 6.4–1 shows the pH range of several types of
natural waters (modified from Nordstrom (1997)—
USGS Training Course: Geochemistry for Groundwa-
ter Systems). Most groundwaters in the United States
have pH values generally ranging from 6.0 to 8.5
(Hem, 1989). Care must be taken when measuring the
pH of groundwaters because the water may be super-
saturated with CO2 before it reaches the land surface,
and degassing can increase pH.
• River waters not affected by contamination generally
have a pH in the range of 6.5 to 8.5 and commonly
exhibit diel fluctuations in pH as a result of photosyn-
thesis, respiration, and temperature, causing variations
in dissolved CO2 (Hem, 1989). Some extreme pH
measurements of waters in the field include -3.6 for
hyperacidic mine waters (Nordstrom and Alpers, 1999),

turns.question: So should we just set our pod's pH alarm at 6.5 to 8.5, since that's what the manual backs up?
turns.answer:
No — I'd advise against that, and I should also correct my previous answer: the excerpt I cited doesn't actually contain that 6.5–8.5 range, so I shouldn't have quoted it. I don't have a document here that gives a general pH range to use as a benchmark.

More importantly, the pod's alert limits aren't meant to be copied from general background values. They start from Clean Earth Rovers defaults and may have been adjusted for your site, and they are alert points, not health standards — so a reading inside them isn't necessarily healthy, and one outside them isn't automatically a problem. Setting an alarm yourself from a manual range could also mean a limit set wider than the sensor can read would never raise an alert.

to compensate for temperature differences at the sampling site.
Again, the accuracy of field measurements should be checked
regularly with buffers equilibrated to the environmental-

the environmental sample is more than ±0.05 pH unit different

meter and electrode should be recalibrated at a temperature
that is ±10 °C of the field-measurement temperature.
For multiparameter sondes that will be deployed for

the recommended procedure is to calibrate in the laboratory

(outside the probe vs. inside the probe) creates a VERY small current. This current
is proportional to the concentration of hydrogen ions in the liquid being measured.

• a thermistor that functions properly and accurately

## 5. Natural Cycles and Look-Alike Events

Rule these out before declaring a pollution event.

### 5.1 Diel (24-Hour) Cycle

- Pattern: DO and pH rise through daylight, peak in mid to late afternoon, and fall overnight to a
  minimum just before dawn. Temperature follows solar heating. ORP shows a weaker version of the
  same pattern, partly because of temperature.
- Diagnostic: DO and pH move in phase, repeat each day, and change smoothly.
- Danger window: The pre-dawn DO minimum. Low-oxygen events and fish kills most often occur
  between about 03:00 and 07:00 local time.
- Caution: Solar-powered DataPods are also most likely to experience low battery voltage in the
  pre-dawn hours. Check battery voltage before interpreting a pre-dawn anomaly (Section 7).

### 5.2 Tidal Cycle

- Pattern: Southern California has mixed semidiurnal tides, with two unequal high tides and two
  unequal low tides per day (the main lunar period is about 12.42 hours). Salinity, temperature, and
  turbidity oscillate with tidal exchange. Turbidity often peaks near maximum current.
- Diagnostic: The change repeats on the tidal clock, not the solar clock, and shifts by about 50
  minutes per day.
- Method: Compare readings to the same tidal phase in the baseline, or remove tidal signal with
  harmonic analysis.
- Sensor exposure: Shallow DataPods may be exposed or nearly exposed at extreme low tides,
  creating fault signatures (Section 7).

### 5.3 Coastal Upwelling (Major False Positive)

- Cause: Winds push surface water offshore, bringing cold, low-oxygen, high-CO₂ deep water to the
  surface. In Southern California, upwelling is strongest in spring (roughly March through June) but
  can occur at other times.
- Signature: Temperature strongly down (2 to 6 °C over one to three days), DO down, pH down,
  salinity slightly up (about 0.1 to 0.3 PSU), ORP slightly down, turbidity little change.
- Why it matters: DO and pH fall together, which resembles organic pollution.
- Diagnostic: Temperature falls with DO and pH. Pollution does not cool the water. Salinity rises
  slightly instead of falling. The pattern often affects several nearby sites at once.

2.3 	Standard pH Buffer Solutions
Standard pH buffer solutions (buffers) are ionic solutions
that are used to calibrate the pH meter and electrodes. Buffers
maintain constant pH values (at a single temperature) because
of their ability to resist changes to the specific pH value for
which they are produced. However, the pH of solutions is
affected by temperature, because the calibration slope (which
is related to the Nernst equation) and the isopotential point
change with temperature. Modern pH meters are typically
calibrated with pH buffers having well-known pH-temper-
ature correlations; quality-assured and National Institute of
Standards and Technology- (NIST) traceable pH buffers are
available from USGS One-Stop1. Most pH meters recognize
the e.m.f. range of certain pH buffers (commonly pH 1.68,
4.01, 7.00, and 10.01 buffers) and are able to automatically
compensate for temperature during calibration. Verify that
the buffers you are using are NIST-traceable, that the values
are recognized correctly by the meter, and that the buffers are
compatible with the ATC for your meter. Consult the manu-
facturer’s manual to be sure that the meter will adjust the
expected value of the buffer for the temperature measured. The
user may be responsible for entering the temperature-adjusted
buffer pH value into the meter for calibration from a chart or
the meter may automatically generate a temperature-adjusted
pH value for the buffer.
Measurements of pH are only as accurate as the buffers
used to calibrate the meter and electrodes.
The commonly used pH buffer solutions and their corre-
sponding pH values from 0 to 90 °C are shown in table 6.4–3.
The pH buffers 1.68, 4.01, and 10.01 are primary standards
(pH values determined by using the standard hydrogen-gas
electrode). Their compositions are typically similar for various
manufacturers; therefore, their variations in pH with tem-
perature are well known. The pH-7.00 buffer is a secondary
standard (pH values determined by interpolation to primary
standards) and its composition (and therefore pH dependence
on temperature) may differ with the manufacturer. However,
the pH-7.00 buffer is typically made either from potassium
dihydrogen phosphate plus sodium hydroxide or from potas-
sium dihydrogen phosphate plus sodium hydrogen phosphate;
the pH values of both buffer formulations are comparable to
within 0.02 pH units from 0 to 90 °C.

No — I'd advise against that, and I should also correct my previous answer: the excerpt I cited doesn't actually contain that 6.5–8.5 range, so I shouldn't have quoted it. I don't have a document here that gives a general pH range to use as a benchmark.

More importantly, the pod's alert limits aren't meant to be copied from general background values. They start from Clean Earth Rovers defaults and may have been adjusted for your site, and they are alert points, not health standards — so a reading inside them isn't necessarily healthy, and one outside them isn't automatically a problem. Setting an alarm yourself from a manual range could also mean a limit set wider than the sensor can read would never raise an alert.

If you want your pod's pH alarm changed or checked, contact Clean Earth Rovers support at sales@cleanearthrovers.com, or your usual contact there if you already work with one.
